newsitem.title: ZAIRE: ZAIRE ACCUSES ANGOLAN TROOPS OF CROSSING BORDER.
newsitem.headline: ZAIRE ACCUSES ANGOLAN TROOPS OF CROSSING BORDER.

text.p: Zaire's beleaguered government has accused neighbouring Angola of invading territory to the west of the capital as it faced continuing rebel advances to the east.

State radio on Friday quoted a presidential statement as saying thousands of traders and local inhabitants had fled the Zairean village of Yema, close to Muanda on the Atlantic coast and about 400 km (240 miles) west of Kinshasa.
The statement said the village was invaded early this week by 1,400 heavily armed soldiers of the Angolan army. Angolan troops were also around Tshikapa, further inland, it said.

With rebels advancing on the capital from the east to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko, the commander of the elite presidential guard (DSP) urged his troops to "fight to your death" to defend Mobutu and the nation.

"Our mission is to protect the head of state, his family, the population, and the whole nation," General Nzimbi Nzale told troops at the Tshatshi military barracks which surrounds Mobutu's Kinshasa residence.

"You want to sell the country away? You don't remember that this is our ancestors' land? You have to defend the country and fight to your death," he railed at the troops in his televised speech, alluding to the tendency of Zairean soldiers to flee at the slightest sign of rebels.
The DSP, Zaire's best-equipped soldiers, are concentrated in and around Kinshasa. Most are from Mobutu's Ngbandi tribe, including Nzimbi who is a close relative of the president.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, whose forces have seized more than half of the vast country, said the battle for Kinshasa would come "sooner than expected and will be very, very swift".
"The force will be big and the firepower overwhelming and necessary to contain the notorious army," he told Reuters in Zaire's second city Lubumbashi on Friday.
The Luanda government has been increasingly linked to Kabila's six-month-old campaign to topple Mobutu who for years backed Angola's UNITA rebels.

For several weeks diplomats and local newspapers have reported the threat of rebels invading areas west of Kinshasa from Zaire's southwestern neighbour, in an attempt to sever the capital from supply routes from its one Atlantic ocean port.

Diplomatic efforts to bring Mobutu and Kabila together before the war reaches the sprawling capital stalled once again on Friday as the two protagonists drifted further apart over the venue for the meeting.

Mobutu's son and spokesman Nzanga Mobutu said his father would have no objection to going to Gabon for talks. Kabila said talks should take place "where security is 100 percent guaranteed" and named South Africa and Zambia as the only options.
In New York, diplomats said Bill Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, was expected to pay a surprise visit to Zaire in an effort to get peace negotiations started.
They said Richardson was likely to leave early in the week and that he hoped to see both Mobuto and Kabila.

Meanwhile one tragic side-effect of the war continued to grab world attention as tens of thousands of Hutu refugees in rebel-held territory were still missing from a camp feared to have been attacked by the Tutsi-led rebels.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan accused the rebels on Friday of carrying out a policy of "slow extermination".
"The secretary-general feels that many innocent people are victims of a policy of slow extermination," Fred Eckhard, Annan's spokesman, said.
"As long as (access) is being intentionally impeded you have to say people are being intentionally allowed to die."
